entries.claim: Describe the change the work should make in the world, and leave the offering itself out of it.
entries.subject: element:product-vision

entries.claim: A vision written on its own, with no strategy beside it, says where to go but not how. Write it as the opening of a strategy, alongside the segments, value proposition and trade-offs.
entries.subject: element:product-vision

entries.claim: Per-product visions nest under the company vision; left unnested they compete with it.
entries.subject: element:product-vision

entries.claim: For [segment] who [need], X is a [category] that [benefit], unlike [alternative].
entries.subject: element:positioning-statement

entries.claim: Brand-led organisations treat this as marketing's asset and product-led ones as product's. Settle ownership before it gets written twice.
entries.subject: element:positioning-statement

entries.claim: Pre-competition work often cannot fill the 'unlike' clause honestly. Leave it empty rather than fake it.
entries.subject: element:positioning-statement

entries.claim: Segment by shared job or behaviour, not demographics alone — demographic-only segments are the classic false-precision trap.
entries.subject: element:customer-segments

entries.claim: In B2B the buyer, the user and the payer differ; healthtech's patient/provider/payer triangle makes single-segment framing misleading.
entries.subject: element:customer-segments

entries.claim: One beachhead segment. A long segment list this early signals unvalidated focus.
entries.subject: element:customer-segments

entries.claim: Distinct from Canonical Model: a segment here is a group of people the offering is for; a category there is one the system uses to sort its own data, such as account types. Ask whether it is about whom we serve or how the system files things.
entries.subject: element:customer-segments

entries.claim: Always relative to the segment's current alternative, including doing nothing.
entries.subject: element:value-proposition

entries.claim: One per segment. A single all-segment value proposition usually means the segments were never really split.
entries.subject: element:value-proposition

entries.claim: Quantify in time, cost or risk. Where there is no market, qualitative is fine — but still name the alternative.
entries.subject: element:value-proposition

entries.claim: Say why now: what changed that makes the work worth doing at this point.
entries.subject: element:case-for-change

entries.claim: Distinct from Value Proposition: the value proposition says why a segment would choose the offering over its alternatives; the case for change says why the work is worth doing now. Ask whose reason it is: the people the offering is for, or whoever commits time and money to the work.
entries.subject: element:case-for-change

entries.claim: Name the problem and whose problem it is, with no solution built in.
entries.subject: element:problem-statement

entries.claim: Solution-shaped problems pre-commit the answer.
entries.subject: element:problem-statement

entries.claim: One quantified pain beats five asserted ones.
entries.subject: element:problem-statement

entries.claim: Distinct from Components & Responsibilities and the other architecture elements. Ask whether a line says what the solution does and how people use it, or how it technically holds together; the second belongs there.
entries.subject: element:solution-overview

entries.claim: A Lean Canvas keeps this deliberately thin — top features only; a design document gives it a full section.
entries.subject: element:solution-overview

entries.claim: State what the solution deliberately does not do. Pairs with Scope (In / Out).
entries.subject: element:solution-overview

entries.claim: List non-goals beside the goals. Each should be something that could reasonably be a goal and is explicitly chosen not to be; a plain negation such as 'the system should not crash' does not count.
entries.subject: element:goals-and-non-goals

entries.claim: Distinct from Success Criteria: a goal names what the work aims at; a success criterion sets the observable threshold, with a date, at which the work counts as having met it. A goal given a number and a date has become a success criterion.
entries.subject: element:goals-and-non-goals

entries.claim: Distinct from Scope (In / Out) and Trade-offs, which also set things aside. Ask what is being set aside: an aim of this work is a non-goal here; a part of the solution goes in Scope's excluded list; a promising direction for the offering as a whole goes in Trade-offs.
entries.subject: element:goals-and-non-goals

entries.claim: Cover every stage at which the offering meets the segment: how they hear of it, weigh it up, buy it, receive it and get support afterwards.
entries.subject: element:channels

entries.claim: Product-led versus sales-led growth is at bottom a channels choice. Regulated and enterprise markets often have imposed channels — brokers, distributors, procurement — that dominate the design.
entries.subject: element:channels

entries.claim: For physical goods, delivery and service channels drive cost structure. Link the two.
entries.subject: element:channels

entries.claim: For each segment, name the kind of relationship: personal assistance, dedicated personal assistance, self-service, automated service, community or co-creation.
entries.subject: element:customer-relationships

entries.claim: Skipping this hides how you keep people once they arrive. For each segment, say what keeps them coming back or staying.
entries.subject: element:customer-relationships

entries.claim: Core to the Business Model Canvas and the Lean Canvas. Strategy canvases often omit it, treating monetisation as downstream of positioning.
entries.subject: element:revenue-streams

entries.claim: In regulated industries this is often fixed by regulation or reimbursement codes. Record it as a constraint, not a choice.
entries.subject: element:revenue-streams

entries.claim: A hypothesis to test, not a plan. Deep tech and hardware commonly defer it until technical maturity.
entries.subject: element:revenue-streams

entries.claim: The dominant driver is the insight, not the line items — services and construction run on per-project labour, software on headcount, hardware on cost of goods sold and capex.
entries.subject: element:cost-structure

entries.claim: Distinguish fixed from variable and note what scales with growth. The growth mechanism can invert the shape.
entries.subject: element:cost-structure

entries.claim: Still applies at personal and household scale, where time is the usual dominant cost.
entries.subject: element:cost-structure

entries.claim: Check all four kinds of key resource: physical, intellectual (brand, patents, data), human and financial.
entries.subject: element:key-resources

entries.claim: Deep tech, EV and robotics are dominated by intellectual property and specialised equipment. Licences and certifications carry lead times — flag them early.
entries.subject: element:key-resources

entries.claim: Software businesses often run thin here. Thin is an answer, not a gap.
entries.subject: element:key-resources

entries.claim: List only what you must do yourselves; any activity someone else does for you belongs in Key Partnerships.
entries.subject: element:key-activities

entries.claim: Distinct from Capabilities: activities are what you do, capabilities are what you must be able to do. Strategy canvases use the latter.
entries.subject: element:key-activities

entries.claim: For each partner, say what you rely on them for, such as supply, integration, resale or a platform you run on.
entries.subject: element:key-partnerships

entries.claim: For platform-dependent products the platform is a partnership with unilateral terms. Track it as a risk too.
entries.subject: element:key-partnerships

entries.claim: In construction and hardware, partner schedules land directly on the critical path.
entries.subject: element:key-partnerships

entries.claim: Test each candidate against the question: could a rival copy it or buy it? Forms that often pass are network effects, proprietary data, switching costs, regulatory protection, patents and brand.
entries.subject: element:unfair-advantage

entries.claim: The Lean Canvas's hardest block — 'first mover' and 'passion' do not qualify.
entries.subject: element:unfair-advantage

entries.claim: Early on there is usually none yet. Write 'none yet' when you looked and found nothing, so a reader can tell it apart from one nobody has considered.
entries.subject: element:unfair-advantage

entries.claim: Record each promising direction the offering refuses. Porter holds that choosing what not to do is the essence of strategy, so a strategy with nothing refused has not yet chosen.
entries.subject: element:trade-offs

entries.claim: Absent from the Business Model Canvas and Lean Canvas by design; core to strategy canvases.
entries.subject: element:trade-offs

entries.claim: Date each refusal and note what it assumed. Revisit it when that changes, for example when a new segment, competitor or capability appears.
entries.subject: element:trade-offs

entries.claim: Name the loop — viral, usage, content, referral, sales-led, paid — rather than writing a generic marketing plan. Loops compound; funnels do not.
entries.subject: element:growth-mechanism

entries.claim: Consumer runs on virality and habit, B2B on expansion revenue and referenceability; regulated growth is often gated by accreditation cycles.
entries.subject: element:growth-mechanism

entries.claim: The gap is the point: capability named minus capability possessed is the hiring, partnering and timeline reality.
entries.subject: element:capabilities

entries.claim: Note the lead time for any ability that is slow to gain, such as a clearance, a certification or a rare skill. It sets the earliest date the strategy can deliver.
entries.subject: element:capabilities

entries.claim: Proxies customer value, not company results. Revenue is an outcome, not a North Star.
entries.subject: element:north-star-metric

entries.claim: One per space, at any abstraction, tested by real users, needs and strategy — never by the org chart. Distinct metrics only for genuinely distinct divisions and customer bases.
entries.subject: element:north-star-metric

entries.claim: A single effort does not get its own North Star. It sets its success criteria on a change in what people do that the effort can influence and that drives the North Star, which Torres calls a product outcome.
entries.subject: element:north-star-metric

entries.claim: A North Star tracks customer value within its framework. The One Metric That Matters identifies the current metric to focus on and may change with the business stage or bottleneck; the names are not interchangeable.
entries.subject: element:north-star-metric

entries.claim: Represents vision and strategy without being either — a strong metric statement lets a reader recover both at a high level.
entries.subject: element:north-star-metric

entries.claim: A North Star without input metrics is not actionable.
entries.subject: element:north-star-metric

entries.claim: Success Metrics owns the definition. A strategy canvas records the choice and links back rather than restating it, because copies drift.
entries.subject: element:north-star-metric

entries.claim: Leading and team-influenceable, or it is an output someone mislabelled.
entries.subject: element:input-metrics

entries.claim: Few and causal beats many and correlated.
entries.subject: element:input-metrics

entries.claim: Where a team already reports KPIs, sort them before reusing any here. Parmenter separates result indicators, which sum up the input of more than one team, from performance indicators, which can be tied to one team; only the second kind can serve as input metrics.
entries.subject: element:input-metrics

entries.claim: The counterweight to any target — latency, churn, quality, trust; burnout at personal scale.
entries.subject: element:guardrail-health-metrics

entries.claim: Guardrails that protect the organisation, such as page-load time or revenue, are largely shared across experiments. Define them once, for the whole organisation, and reuse them in every effort.
entries.subject: element:guardrail-health-metrics

entries.claim: Experimentation-heavy organisations formalise these as launch blockers; everywhere else they stay implicit until an incident. Write them down first.
entries.subject: element:guardrail-health-metrics

entries.claim: Distinct from Input Metrics. Ask whether the number should move or hold: an input metric is pushed to move, a guardrail is held within its range. Neither the Business Model Canvas nor the Lean Canvas has a block for guardrails, so keep them in Success Metrics.
entries.subject: element:guardrail-health-metrics

entries.claim: 'Improve X' invites post-hoc rationalisation. Set a threshold and a measurement date.
entries.subject: element:success-criteria

entries.claim: Per-initiative acceptance, set before the work, expiring with the effort — unlike metrics that run continuously.
entries.subject: element:success-criteria

entries.claim: A product requirements document's launch 'success metrics' and an OKR's key results belong here: each is a threshold with a date, usually on an input metric.
entries.subject: element:success-criteria

entries.claim: Point to the shared measures the work must not break instead of copying them, and state in full each threshold this work commits to.
entries.subject: element:success-criteria

entries.claim: Run top-down and bottom-up. They should disagree, and reconciling them is the insight.
entries.subject: element:market-sizing

entries.claim: As much an investor convention as a planning one. Include it only when the bet's size justifies it.
entries.subject: element:market-sizing

entries.claim: Pre-category, point estimates are fiction. Use scenario ranges.
entries.subject: element:market-sizing

entries.claim: Size the share the offering could realistically win as well as the whole market. The whole market on its own overstates the opportunity.
entries.subject: element:market-sizing

entries.claim: Distinct from Capabilities: this audits the strengths and weaknesses we have now, judged against the work; Capabilities names the abilities a strategy requires, including those still to gain.
entries.subject: element:internal-strengths-weaknesses

entries.claim: Sanitised weaknesses are the most common SWOT failure.
entries.subject: element:internal-strengths-weaknesses

entries.claim: Strengths only count against a stated goal or competitor. Context-free strengths are trivia.
entries.subject: element:internal-strengths-weaknesses

entries.claim: Distinct from Macro-Environment Factors, which lists outside conditions lens by lens; this judges which of them, and which competitor moves, help or threaten the work. The same law may appear in both: once as a fact, once as a threat with an owner.
entries.subject: element:external-opportunities-threats

entries.claim: Draw each opportunity and threat from the PESTLE scan or the competitor profiles, and say which one it came from.
entries.subject: element:external-opportunities-threats

entries.claim: A threat with no owner and no trigger gets noticed only once it lands. Carry each threat that needs a response into Risks & Assumptions, where it gets an owner.
entries.subject: element:external-opportunities-threats

entries.claim: Six lenses: political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental.
entries.subject: element:macro-environment-factors

entries.claim: Weight by industry — legal and political dominate banking and healthtech, environmental dominates construction and energy, social and technological dominate consumer.
entries.subject: element:macro-environment-factors

entries.claim: Review it after an election, a new law or regulation, or a change in the platforms or technology the work depends on.
entries.subject: element:macro-environment-factors

entries.claim: Where a condition fixes a limit the work must meet, record it in Constraints too.
entries.subject: element:macro-environment-factors

entries.claim: For a lens that was checked and holds nothing that affects the work, write 'nothing found', so a reader can tell it apart from a lens nobody checked.
entries.subject: element:macro-environment-factors

entries.claim: Per alternative: what it offers, segment overlap, how well it serves those people, pricing where knowable.
entries.subject: element:competitor-profile

entries.claim: Include indirect alternatives and doing nothing. The spreadsheet-and-email incumbent beats most challengers.
entries.subject: element:competitor-profile

entries.claim: Sales battlecards are the externalised descendant. Keep evidence separate from spin.
entries.subject: element:competitor-profile

entries.claim: Distinct from User / Job Stories: a job holds whatever solution is chosen; a story says what the solution lets a person do. A when / want / so-that line written before any solution exists states a job.
entries.subject: element:jobs-to-be-done

entries.claim: Jobs are circumstance-anchored and stable. Solutions churn; jobs do not.
entries.subject: element:jobs-to-be-done

entries.claim: The when / want / so-that job-story form captures circumstance better than persona-attached stories.
entries.subject: element:jobs-to-be-done

entries.claim: Osterwalder's value-proposition-canvas pairing — pains before, gains after.
entries.subject: element:pains-and-gains

entries.claim: Distinct from Problem Statement: this records what each segment finds frustrating and hopes for, many entries drawn from evidence; Problem Statement names the one problem the work chooses to solve.
entries.subject: element:pains-and-gains

entries.claim: Distinct from Jobs to Be Done: the job is the progress itself; pains are what gets in the way of making it today, and gains are what would make it better.
entries.subject: element:pains-and-gains

entries.claim: Source from evidence — interviews, support logs — not empathy-map guessing. Rank by severity times frequency or the list flattens.
entries.subject: element:pains-and-gains

entries.claim: A user story (as-a / I-want / so-that) presumes a persona; a job story (when / I-want / so-I-can) presumes a circumstance. Pick one per document; do not mix.
entries.subject: element:user-job-stories

entries.claim: Acceptance criteria turn a story from a conversation-starter into testable scope.
entries.subject: element:user-job-stories

entries.claim: Distinct from Jobs to Be Done: ask whether the line names what the solution must let a person do. A story does, and acceptance criteria test it; the job behind it stays true whatever is built.
entries.subject: element:user-job-stories

entries.claim: Distinct from User / Job Stories: a story says what the solution should let a person do, one capability at a time; a trace follows one person through the solution in one circumstance, step by step, joins included.
entries.subject: element:stepwise-trace

entries.claim: The joins are the content. No single story contains a seam, and a set of stories does not sum to one trace.
entries.subject: element:stepwise-trace

entries.claim: Distinct from Solution Overview: a trace follows one person in one concrete circumstance in full detail; the overview outlines all the behaviour at once. Ask whether the text follows one path or covers them all. In a design document, refer to the trace where the RFC template puts its guide-level explanation.
entries.subject: element:stepwise-trace

entries.claim: For an assumption, state what is being relied on and how it will be checked. For a risk, state what could happen, its significance, and the response.
entries.subject: element:risks-and-assumptions

entries.claim: Distinct from Opportunities & Threats: there an outside condition is judged for planning; here anything inside or outside that could harm the work gets a response and someone to handle it.
entries.subject: element:risks-and-assumptions

entries.claim: Before committing, imagine the work has already failed and have each person write down why. This brings out risks people hesitate to raise.
entries.subject: element:risks-and-assumptions

entries.claim: The RFC tradition records drawbacks — known, accepted costs — separately from risks, which are uncertainties.
entries.subject: element:risks-and-assumptions

entries.claim: Where an approver or regulator will review the work, date each entry and name its owner and response, so the record can be audited.
entries.subject: element:risks-and-assumptions

entries.claim: Three lists, not two: included, deferred with a revisit trigger, and excluded with the reason.
entries.subject: element:scope-in-out

entries.claim: Distinct from Trade-offs: scope excludes parts of the solution for this work; Trade-offs refuses directions for the offering as a whole.
entries.subject: element:scope-in-out

entries.claim: The excluded list is the valuable one — it prevents silent re-expansion.
entries.subject: element:scope-in-out

entries.claim: The deferred list is where natural extensions land — the RFC tradition's future possibilities.
entries.subject: element:scope-in-out

entries.claim: Imposed, not chosen: regulation, budget, deadline, platform, physics.
entries.subject: element:constraints

entries.claim: Distinct from Cross-Cutting Concerns: a constraint is an imposed limit on the work that no design choice moves — budget, deadline, platform, what the law allows; a cross-cutting concern is an obligation every part of the solution must be designed to meet — security, privacy, accessibility. One law can supply both: a limit here, a property demanded throughout there.
entries.subject: element:constraints

entries.claim: Distinct from Trade-offs. Mislabelling a choice as a constraint hides a decision.
entries.subject: element:constraints

entries.claim: At minimum, say how the solution handles security, privacy and observability (how you will see what it is doing once it runs). Design docs at Google use this section to make sure these are always taken into consideration.
entries.subject: element:cross-cutting-concerns

entries.claim: Regulated domains extend the list — compliance, audit, accessibility.
entries.subject: element:cross-cutting-concerns

entries.claim: Exists so these get weighed while change is still cheap.
entries.subject: element:cross-cutting-concerns

entries.claim: Take accessibility requirements from WCAG 2.2, whose success criteria can each be tested; normal text, for example, needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. They apply to the brand's colours and type like everything else.
entries.subject: element:cross-cutting-concerns

entries.claim: Distinct from Verbal Identity Rules: marks, colour, type and imagery, and how the name is drawn as a logotype, are look; words, voice, naming, standing copy, and how the name is spelled, cased and punctuated in text, are wording. A trademark policy usually splits across both.
entries.subject: element:visual-identity-rules

entries.claim: A rule set with nothing forbidden is usually not settled yet.
entries.subject: element:visual-identity-rules

entries.claim: Mood boards help a team agree on a feeling before any rule exists, and get copied into the rules by mistake. Record only what was adopted: the final colours, type and marks.
entries.subject: element:visual-identity-rules

entries.claim: The machine-readable form fixes the order the sections come in, and requires none of them except a primary colour palette.
entries.subject: element:visual-identity-rules

entries.claim: Token formats carry colour, size, type and timing. Icons, accessibility and writing rules fit in none of them, and are no less settled for that.
entries.subject: element:visual-identity-rules

entries.claim: Name a specific reference rather than a list of adjectives. 'Modern, clean, premium' fits almost anything.
entries.subject: element:visual-identity-rules

entries.claim: Distinct from Cross-Cutting Concerns: here go the brand's standing rules for its look; a record that one design meets an obligation such as accessibility goes there. Ask whether the line sets a rule for all material or checks one piece of work.
entries.subject: element:visual-identity-rules

entries.claim: Most of these are only partly answered. A settled palette and nothing else is a real answer, not a stub.
entries.subject: element:visual-identity-rules

entries.claim: Writing sits among the foundations as a peer of colour and typography, not beneath them.
entries.subject: element:verbal-identity-rules

entries.claim: Where the guide is split into a visual branch and a content or messaging branch, as GitLab's Pajamas is, put these rules in the content branch.
entries.subject: element:verbal-identity-rules

entries.claim: The words a brand refuses do as much work as the ones it adopts.
entries.subject: element:verbal-identity-rules

entries.claim: Distinct from Positioning Statement and Value Proposition: here goes the approved wording itself, such as boilerplate, taglines and pitches of set lengths. Ask whether you are fixing words or deciding what to claim; deciding what to claim belongs there, and the wording here draws on it without restating it.
entries.subject: element:verbal-identity-rules

entries.claim: Where wording is decided case by case and no rules exist, note that here, so a reader can tell it apart from rules that exist but have not been collected.
entries.subject: element:verbal-identity-rules

entries.claim: Describe and compare the options here, including the chosen option. Decision records the commitment and why it was chosen.
entries.subject: element:alternatives-considered

entries.claim: Standard in RFCs, decision documents and decision records. Describe the options considered, including the chosen option.
entries.subject: element:alternatives-considered

entries.claim: Naming the rejected options is grammatically obligatory in the Y-statement form — 'and neglected …' — not an optional courtesy to the reader.
entries.subject: element:alternatives-considered

entries.claim: Check that the options are feasible, diverse and comprehensive: each could really be done, none is a small variant of another, and together they cover the realistic ways to solve the problem.
entries.subject: element:alternatives-considered

entries.claim: Flanking a preferred course with two deliberately unattractive alternatives simulates choice rather than offering it.
entries.subject: element:alternatives-considered

entries.claim: Two honest alternatives beat five straw men. Absence invites re-litigation.
entries.subject: element:alternatives-considered

entries.claim: Give each criterion its weight or rank, so a reader can see how conflicting criteria were balanced. State it before the options are scored, not inside the decision's reasoning.
entries.subject: element:decision-criteria

entries.claim: Criteria are a first-class object, not prose inside the rationale: options are assessed against them, and the assessment carries a sign. That is what lets a later reader see that two decisions were judged against the same criterion, or against conflicting ones.
entries.subject: element:decision-criteria

entries.claim: Where an outside body may review the decision, name every factor that was balanced and say how each entered the decision. A US Record of Decision had to do exactly this.
entries.subject: element:decision-criteria

entries.claim: Distinct from Goals & Non-Goals and from Constraints: a criterion is a dimension options are compared along, a goal is an outcome aimed for, and a constraint is a fixed limit that admits no trade-off.
entries.subject: element:decision-criteria

entries.claim: Honestly empty means the choice was made on one dominant consideration already stated in the decision — not that the criteria were never articulated.
entries.subject: element:decision-criteria

entries.claim: Distinct from Accepted Consequences: the decision states what is chosen and why ('we drop the evening track because only four signed up'); a consequence is what the choice brings that we accept ('tutors lose Thursday income'). Stating what is chosen is the decision even when it reads as a loss.
entries.subject: element:decision

entries.claim: One decision per record, dated, and never edited in place: a stale decision is superseded by a new record.
entries.subject: element:decision

entries.claim: Bad rationale has a recognisable shape — 'everybody does it', 'we have always done it like that', 'this will look good on my resume'. Reasoning that survives none of those is not reasoning.
entries.subject: element:decision

entries.claim: Give the reasons beside the choice, and name the criteria the chosen option met best. MADR's template allows the outcome to cite its decision drivers in this way.
entries.subject: element:decision

entries.claim: Name the objective or requirement the decision serves. If it serves none, question whether it needs making at all.
entries.subject: element:decision

entries.claim: All consequences belong here, not only the favourable ones — positive, negative and neutral alike. The consequences of one decision commonly become the context of the next.
entries.subject: element:accepted-consequences

entries.claim: Distinct from Reversal Condition: a consequence is what the decision brings, known and accepted when it is taken; a reversal condition is an observation not yet made that would reopen it. A consequence turning out worse than accepted is one such observation.
entries.subject: element:accepted-consequences

entries.claim: Distinct from Trade-offs: a trade-off is a promising direction the offering refuses as part of its strategy; a consequence follows from one decision already taken and is accepted with it. If the entry traces back to a specific decision, it belongs here.
entries.subject: element:accepted-consequences

entries.claim: Distinct from Risks & Assumptions: a consequence is accepted and expected, a risk is uncertain. Filing a known cost as a risk hides that someone chose it.
entries.subject: element:accepted-consequences

entries.claim: An option can outperform every alternative and still have consequences. Distinguish none identified from not assessed; neither follows from the option dominating the comparison.
entries.subject: element:accepted-consequences

entries.claim: An observable condition, not a review date: what would have to be seen for this to stop holding. 'Revisit in six months' is a calendar entry; 'if median latency exceeds the budget for two consecutive quarters' is a condition.
entries.subject: element:reversal-condition

entries.claim: Checking that a decision was implemented and deciding whether it should change are different activities. Implementation compliance is not itself a condition for reconsideration.
entries.subject: element:reversal-condition

entries.claim: Record uncertainty that may warrant revisiting the decision. New evidence or changed circumstances can justify reconsideration regardless of its original confidence.
entries.subject: element:reversal-condition

entries.claim: Distinct from Risks & Assumptions: a failing assumption is one trigger among several. A better alternative appearing, a constraint lifting, or an authority changing reopen the decision without any assumption having failed.
entries.subject: element:reversal-condition

entries.claim: State what would warrant reconsideration. If no trigger has been identified, say so; this does not establish that the commitment is irreversible.
entries.subject: element:reversal-condition

entries.claim: Say what each precedent teaches the work: what to copy and what to avoid. A list of look-alikes with no lesson is not prior art.
entries.subject: element:prior-art

entries.claim: A standard RFC section: precedent survey across other systems, organisations or communities.
entries.subject: element:prior-art

entries.claim: Distinct from Competitor Profile: that grades how well each alternative serves the people the offering is for; this draws lessons from how others solved similar problems, whether or not they compete. Absence invites reinvention.
entries.subject: element:prior-art

entries.claim: Give each stage its audience, such as a pilot group, a wider beta or everyone, and the observation that would stop or roll back the rollout before the next stage.
entries.subject: element:rollout-and-phasing

entries.claim: Distinct from Sequence & Foreclosure: rollout stages how widely the solution is introduced, with a stopping condition per stage; sequence orders the work's own steps by what each forecloses.
entries.subject: element:rollout-and-phasing

entries.claim: Enterprise implementation practice treats this as a core deliverable section. Product briefs include it only when release risk warrants.
entries.subject: element:rollout-and-phasing

entries.claim: Sort the steps by whether they can be walked back. A step you can reverse is a two-way door and deserves speed; a step you cannot is a one-way door and deserves deliberation. Applying the heavy process to everything is as costly a mistake as applying the light one to the irreversible.
entries.subject: element:sequence-and-foreclosure

entries.claim: Name what each step forecloses, not merely what it enables. An order that closes no doors is a preference, not a sequence.
entries.subject: element:sequence-and-foreclosure

entries.claim: Honestly empty means every step is independently reversible in any order — in which case say so, because that is the licence to move fast.
entries.subject: element:sequence-and-foreclosure

entries.claim: Each wants an owner and a resolution path. An unowned question is a risk mislabelled.
entries.subject: element:open-questions

entries.claim: Distinct from Risks & Assumptions: an open question is something to answer before a point can be settled; an assumption is a belief the work proceeds on and checks along the way. Proceeding without the answer turns the question into an assumption.
entries.subject: element:open-questions

entries.claim: Compare the list across drafts: it should get shorter. A list that keeps growing means the work is not yet ready to settle.
entries.subject: element:open-questions

entries.claim: Write 'none open' only when every question raised has been answered or recorded as an assumption, so a reader can tell it apart from a list nobody has drawn up.
entries.subject: element:open-questions

entries.claim: C4 level 1: the system, its users, and the external systems it exchanges with.
entries.subject: element:system-boundary-and-context

entries.claim: The boundary is a security and ownership decision, not just a drawing choice.
entries.subject: element:system-boundary-and-context

entries.claim: Give each part one responsibility you can state in a single sentence. If the sentence needs an 'and', consider splitting the part.
entries.subject: element:components-and-responsibilities

entries.claim: Drawing the parts of the system on a diagram meant to show only the system and its surroundings makes that diagram hard to read. Keep the system context diagram to the system as one box, and show its parts in the Architecture Overview.
entries.subject: element:components-and-responsibilities

entries.claim: Components run and own behaviour. The named categories the system reasons with are Canonical Model.
entries.subject: element:components-and-responsibilities

entries.claim: Flows name the contract — API, event, file — and the contract's owner.
entries.subject: element:data-flows-and-integrations

entries.claim: In regulated and privacy contexts flows are compliance surface. Annotate data classification — personally identifiable information, protected health information — where it applies.
entries.subject: element:data-flows-and-integrations

entries.claim: Give each category its identifier and the fields its entries carry, so the model fixes the shape of an entry and not only its name.
entries.subject: element:canonical-model

entries.claim: Use each category's name the same way everywhere: in conversation, in documents and in the system itself. Keep it stable once other parts depend on it.
entries.subject: element:canonical-model

entries.claim: Record the categories and their fields, with only as many example entries as a reader needs to understand them. A full list of entries is the offering's data and belongs with it.
entries.subject: element:canonical-model

entries.claim: Documents that use these categories refer to this model for them, so each category is defined in one place.
entries.subject: element:canonical-model

entries.claim: Distinct from Revenue Streams: funding pays for the work; revenue is what the offering earns from the people who take it up. Where the offering's own earnings pay for the work, name them here as the source and describe them there.
entries.subject: element:funding-source

entries.claim: Record each funder's conditions. Where a condition limits the work, also list it under Constraints, pointing back here instead of restating it.
entries.subject: element:funding-source

entries.claim: Count time and in-kind support as funding where no money changes hands. In personal work the funder is usually yourself, in time or savings; write that down, because it is an answer.
entries.subject: element:funding-source

entries.claim: For each approval, name who gives it and who gave them the right to give it. If nobody holds that right, close the gap before relying on the approval.
entries.subject: element:decision-authority-and-approvals

entries.claim: Distinct from Consent & Authority: an approval is a decision someone takes over whether the work goes ahead; a licence, permit, consent or legal basis is the permission the work holds. A regulator can appear in both: as an approval here, as its clearance there.
entries.subject: element:decision-authority-and-approvals

entries.claim: If the work needs no one's approval, say so and say how you know, for example that the spend is within your own authority. A blank list with no such note reads as not yet checked.
entries.subject: element:decision-authority-and-approvals

entries.claim: List everyone who bears a cost, hazard or loss from the work, including people who never use what it produces, such as the neighbours of a building site.
entries.subject: element:affected-and-interested-parties

entries.claim: If the work's effects fall only on those accountable for it, say so and leave the list empty for that reason. A blank list with no such note cannot show that anyone checked who else carries the work's risks.
entries.subject: element:affected-and-interested-parties

entries.claim: For each party, record what claim it has to be heard, such as a legal right, a contract or direct harm. That claim decides whether a risk it carries can be accepted without asking it.
entries.subject: element:affected-and-interested-parties

entries.claim: Distinct from Decision Authority & Approvals: a party here is heard and weighed; an approver there decides whether the work goes ahead. If the work needs their yes, list them there.
entries.subject: element:affected-and-interested-parties

entries.claim: Record each finding with how precisely it was measured and when it was observed. An undated survey cannot say whether it still holds.
entries.subject: element:as-built-survey

entries.claim: Distinct from Constraints: the survey records what is actually in place; a constraint is a limit imposed on the work. A measured clearance is a finding here; a rule forbidding building into it is a constraint.
entries.subject: element:as-built-survey

entries.claim: Name the observation that would show the prediction wrong. A prediction no observation could contradict is not testable.
entries.subject: element:hypothesis

entries.claim: Distinct from Success Criteria: a success criterion says what counts as the work succeeding; a hypothesis says what the world will show. A test that refutes its hypothesis can still succeed as work, by settling the question.
entries.subject: element:hypothesis

entries.claim: Distinct from Risks & Assumptions: an assumption is something the work relies on; a hypothesis is a prediction stated so a test can show it wrong. Testing an assumption states it as a hypothesis here; the assumption stays in the register until the test settles it.
entries.subject: element:hypothesis

entries.claim: Fix the procedure before any data are collected, and say for each thing the prediction names how it becomes a measured quantity: instrument, unit, sample and who records it. A procedure changed after the data arrive turns the test into exploration.
entries.subject: element:measurement-protocol

entries.claim: The opening Overview of a DESIGN.md carries this: personality, audience and the response the brand should evoke. It is what to fall back on when no rule covers a case.
entries.subject: element:brand-character

entries.claim: No standard form fixes this canvas's blocks. Always fill in the vision, segments, value proposition, cost structure, trade-offs, capabilities and the North Star it steers by; once the bet is proven, also the growth mechanism and unfair advantage. Add any other block only when it changes what the offering will aim for or refuse next.
entries.subject: artifact:product-strategy-canvas

entries.claim: Fill in all nine blocks: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships and cost structure.
entries.subject: artifact:business-model-canvas

entries.claim: When a block does not apply, keep it and write in it why it does not apply.
entries.subject: artifact:business-model-canvas

entries.claim: For a new business every block is still a guess, and this canvas checks that the guesses fit together. The Lean Canvas picks which guess to test first; the Startup Canvas commits the venture's aims.
entries.subject: artifact:business-model-canvas

entries.claim: A one-page adaptation of the Business Model Canvas for ventures under extreme uncertainty.
entries.subject: artifact:lean-canvas

entries.claim: Fill in each of these blocks: problem, customer segments, unique value proposition, solution, channels, revenue streams, cost structure, key metrics and unfair advantage.
entries.subject: artifact:lean-canvas

entries.claim: When a block does not apply, keep it and write in it why it does not apply.
entries.subject: artifact:lean-canvas

entries.claim: The Lean Canvas picks which assumption to test before customers have paid; this canvas commits a forming venture's aims and how it will make money.
entries.subject: artifact:startup-canvas

entries.claim: Distinct from a sales battlecard, which is written from this analysis to win deals. Ask whether an entry reports how well an alternative serves people or argues for the offering; arguments belong on the battlecard.
entries.subject: artifact:competitor-analysis

entries.claim: Keep it to one or two pages about the problem, written before any product requirements document.
entries.subject: artifact:opportunity-assessment

entries.claim: The risk register is standard across PMBOK, PRINCE2 and ISO Guide 73 — a record of information about identified risks.
entries.subject: artifact:risk-assessment

entries.claim: Canonical sections: context and scope, goals and non-goals, the actual design, alternatives considered, cross-cutting concerns. Skip the document when the solution is unambiguous.
entries.subject: artifact:design-doc

entries.claim: Most large projects start with a PRD to define the problem, followed by an RFC to propose a solution.
entries.subject: artifact:design-doc

entries.claim: The request-for-discussion is the same document family, inspired by the IETF's RFC series.
entries.subject: artifact:design-doc

entries.claim: Do not mistake this for a Solution Design Document, an enterprise-implementation deliverable whose content belongs in the Architecture Overview. A design doc proposes one approach for reviewers to agree to or object to.
entries.subject: artifact:design-doc

entries.claim: Brand values and purpose belong in the Product Vision and the Positioning Statement. Ask whether a passage says what the brand stands for (put it there) or how the brand should feel and be expressed in look and wording (keep it here).
entries.subject: artifact:brand-identity-guide

entries.claim: Brand guidelines, a brand book and a style guide all count as this guide when they set the brand's intended feeling and its rules for look and wording, whatever the document is called.
entries.subject: artifact:brand-identity-guide

entries.claim: DESIGN.md represents visual design-system rules. It can supply the visual portion of a brand guide; it does not represent its verbal rules.
entries.subject: artifact:brand-identity-guide

entries.claim: Instructions for revising the document are not part of the document. That is a process, and it belongs wherever the process is owned.
entries.subject: artifact:brand-identity-guide

entries.claim: Stale when an adopted colour, typeface, logo or other brand asset changes. A guide that shows a look nobody uses any more misleads more confidently than having no guide.
entries.subject: artifact:brand-identity-guide

entries.claim: Follow one person pursuing one goal, step by step. Use it early to settle what the solution should do, and leave detailed interface design out.
entries.subject: artifact:scenario-walkthrough

entries.claim: Three unrelated practices share the name: a live usability test with users, an architecture review of quality attributes (ATAM), and a document or code inspection meeting. The walkthrough meant here is a written step-by-step trace of one person reaching one goal; if yours is a meeting or a test session, it is one of the others.
entries.subject: artifact:scenario-walkthrough

entries.claim: The North Star Metric and the input metrics that drive it.
entries.subject: artifact:success-metrics

entries.claim: C4 levels 1 and 2 — system context and containers.
entries.subject: artifact:architecture-overview

entries.claim: Record only the flows that cross the system's boundary; flows between the system's own parts belong in the Architecture Overview.
entries.subject: artifact:system-context-diagram

entries.claim: Show people and external systems at C4 level 1. Use the Architecture Overview for internal containers and their interactions at level 2. C4 component-level detail is a further level.
entries.subject: artifact:system-context-diagram

entries.claim: Exactly one named decider. Without one, a brief produces discussion rather than a decision.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-brief

entries.claim: Beside the decider, list who contributes and who is only informed: contributors give input, those informed do not. Neither decides.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-brief

entries.claim: The framing carries a date and the reason for that date. Without a deadline, the brief is only a discussion document.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-brief

entries.claim: Quality is judged before the outcome is known, on the frame, the alternatives, the information, the criteria and trade-offs, the reasoning, and the commitment to act — and is no better than the weakest of them.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-brief

entries.claim: Finish with a commitment step: until the choice is voiced it is not taken.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-brief

entries.claim: Agreement obtained privately and never voiced does not bind, and the decision reopens the first time it meets friction.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-brief

entries.claim: Distinct from the Decision Record, which it feeds. Ask whether the choice is still to be made: while it is, the criteria and options belong in this brief; once it is made, the Decision Record keeps the options that were rejected and why.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-brief

entries.claim: Distinct from the Opportunity Assessment, which asks whether to pursue one thing at all, and from the Design Doc, which offers one approach to react to. This one picks among several.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-brief

entries.claim: It goes stale the moment the decision is taken. Stop editing it then: changing it afterwards reopens a settled choice against criteria that have since moved.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-brief

entries.claim: One decision per record — context, decision, status, consequences — with status moving proposed to accepted to deprecated or superseded.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-record

entries.claim: The set of records is an append-only log. An accepted record is not edited; a changed decision is a new record that supersedes the old one, with the two linked, so the history of the thinking survives the change of direction.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-record

entries.claim: Write a record when someone will later need the reasoning without its author there to explain it, or when the decision would be costly to undo.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-record

entries.claim: ISO 42010 weighs a decision by impact and cost of change: many stakeholders affected, expensive to enforce, costly to reverse, non-obvious reasoning, major expenditure. Only one of those is about architecture.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-record

entries.claim: The form is not architecture-specific and never was. The same record shape serves a pricing, hiring or procurement decision; what changes with the domain is which decisions merit a record and what the record points at.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-record

entries.claim: A decision record that grows into a design guide has stopped being a decision record.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-record

entries.claim: Reassess when an observation named in the Reversal Condition occurs, or when the circumstances the decision rested on change. If the condition cannot be checked, find out what evidence is missing.
entries.subject: artifact:decision-record

elements.question: What lasting change should the work make?
Which kind of offering should each segment see ours as?
Exactly which groups is the offering for?
Why would a segment choose the offering over its alternatives?
Why is the work worth doing now?
What problem should the work solve?
What is the intended solution, in outline?
Which goals does the work pursue?
How does the offering reach each segment?
What kind of relationship do we keep with each segment?
How does the offering earn money?
Who funds the work?
What mainly determines the cost of providing the offering?
What assets must we own or control?
Which activities must we perform ourselves?
What do we deliberately rely on others for?
What advantage of ours is hard for others to copy or buy?
Which promising directions do we refuse?
How does the offering's growth produce more growth?
Which abilities must we have or gain?
What one measure best shows the value people get from the offering?
Which measures within our control predict the value people get from the offering?
Which measures must stay within set ranges while we pursue other targets?
What observable result counts as success for the work?
How large is the market the offering could serve?
Which of our own strengths and weaknesses matter to the work?
Which outside opportunities and threats matter to the work?
Which political, economic, social, technological, legal or environmental conditions affect the work?
How well does each alternative serve the people the offering is for?
What is a person trying to achieve?
What frustrations and hoped-for gains does each segment have?
What should the solution let a person do?
What happens at each step of one path through the solution?
What could harm the work if it happened or proved wrong?
Who does the work affect beyond those accountable for it?
Whose approval does the work need?
What licence, permit, consent or legal basis allows the work?
What do we include in the solution now, defer, or exclude?
What imposed limits apply to the work?
What do measurements of the existing state show?
Which requirements must every part of the solution meet?
What are the rules for the brand's look?
What are the rules for the brand's wording?
What feeling should the brand's look and wording create?
Which options do we consider?
By what criteria do we judge the options?
What did we decide?
What consequences of the decision do we accept?
What observation would reopen the decision?
What testable prediction do we make?
How do we measure each thing the prediction names?
How have others solved problems like ours?
In what stages do we introduce the solution?
In what order must the work proceed?
Which questions about the work remain open?
What is the system itself responsible for?
What is each part of the system responsible for?
What data moves where?
Which named categories does the system use?

frames.question: Which stage of the work is this part of?

values.question: Who are we, where are we going, and why that way?
What is worth solving, for whom, and is it viable?
What are we building and how does it behave?
How do we know it works?
How does it technically hold together?
How is this carried out and kept working?

frames.question: Who has to reconstruct this reasoning without the author present?
Can this step be undone, and at what cost?
How do people come to take up the offering?

values.question: Does it arrive whether or not they'd choose it?
Do they take it up only by deciding to, with nothing to pay?
Is paying how they take it up?

frames.question: Who has to be asked or told before the work goes ahead?

values.question: Can the work go ahead without asking or telling anyone?
Is asking someone first a courtesy you may skip?
Must someone be told first, with no yes needed?
Does someone's yes have to come first?
Does a law or regulator require a yes first?

frames.question: How settled is the bet this work rests on?
What kind of thing does this work produce?
Who is this artifact going to?

overview.covers: The reasoning around deliberate work — what makes it worth doing, what it should be, and whether it held up. The work may produce something made or put in place, a service rendered, or something learned; for a recipient — including your own later self — who simply receives it, free to take it or leave it, or paying for it.
overview.excludes: Doing or delivering the work itself.
overview.for: Whoever is accountable for that judgement or has to account for it later — one person on one machine, a group, or an organisation.

terms.means: The deliberate effort itself, from deciding it is worth doing to checking whether it worked.
The result that reaches the people the work is for, such as a product, a service or a finding.
The planned answer to the need, with its parts.
The parts of the solution and the connections between them.
A group of people the offering is for, who share a need or circumstance.
